summary.title: 7 Absolute Truths I Unlearned as Junior Developer
summary.one_liner: Seven common beliefs junior developers hold about titles, testing, tech FOMO, code quality, documentation, technical debt and seniority, and what the author learned instead.
takeaways: Years of experience is not the same as the right kind of experience; a supportive team with code review teaches far more than working alone.
Many companies, even well-known ones, have legacy code and minimal tests; conference talks often show proof-of-concepts rather than real systems.
Messy code is not automatically technical debt; debt slows you down and some debt is a healthy, deliberate trade-off.
Prefer automation such as tests over extensive documentation, which can go stale; architecture matters more than small style nitpicks.
Seniority requires many skills beyond programming, such as communication, estimation, and collaboration, and admitting what you don't know.
summary.summary: The author, a developer with about ten years of professional experience, reflects on seven beliefs she held as a junior developer and how each shifted. Each section pairs a personal anecdote (such as a first job title, a startup with no tests, or 800 linting errors fixed by hand) with a 'what I eventually learned' section. The tone is informal and personal rather than technical, with no code samples. It is aimed at both junior and senior developers.
